evidence.claims: Backed: forward factor 4.7-5.6 (results.txt and my mesh study, 4.58 at 2 layers), deflections 0.14/0.94/4.45/15.5 mm (my beam check), the 2.5 and 3.0 mm designs failing stress and deflection (nominal 402/846 MPa, deflection 4.45/15.5 mm), masses, min wall 1.2 mm met (min(b,w)=1.5). Unbacked or contradicted: (1) README.md:37 and research/README.md:560 'the 2.0 mm design passes only on the coarse mesh ... its verdict depends on the mesh': the coarse 95.7 MPa is the stress w/4 inside the outer fibre (mid-arm coarse value 83.5 vs 162.8 converged), so it is a recovery artefact, not a credible pass. (2) README.md:42 'peak stresses ... probably overstate what a real filleted part sees': every reported FE peak (36.7-676.0) is below the beam-theory stress with no concentration (57.3-845.9), so they understate it. (3) README.md:39 'finer-mesh peaks about 1.5x the coarse ones' is presented as a corner-singularity effect; 1.5 = 0.75/0.5, the ratio of centroid positions for nw=4 vs nw=2. (4) README.md:38 '1.5 mm passes every check ... stress 37 to 57 MPa': the nominal 57.3 passes, but the corner value rises to 74.1 at nw=8 and is still climbing, so a real fillet (Peterson Kt about 1.5-2.5 for small r) could exceed 100 MPa: not established either way. The headline verdict (only 1.5 mm survives) is right because the nominal stress alone decides it. 'Stylised and preliminary', 'assumed limits' and the AI-assistance note are present.
evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it? Little. It is one step in a cluster of 58 simdesign-* directories that research/PROGRAMMES.md:8-17 itself names as the fragmentation problem ('over 20 simdesign-* projects probe the mesh behaviour of one laser-cut bracket'). Nearest prior work, none cited: Williams (1952) for the re-entrant-corner stress singularity (why a sharp-corner peak has no converged value); Peterson's Stress Concentration Factors (Pilkey & Pilkey, 3rd ed. 2008) for the filleted corner it defers; Zienkiewicz & Zhu (1992) superconvergent patch recovery and NAFEMS benchmark practice for stress recovery; Timoshenko & Gere for lateral-torsional buckling of the narrow arm. The result (beam theory says only the widest design meets 100 MPa) follows from a one-line hand calculation; the FE adds a buckling confirmation but its stress numbers would mislead a reader.
evidence.domain: Against standard FE stress-assessment practice (evaluate stress at the outer fibre by nodal extrapolation or superconvergent recovery, check FE against beam theory away from discontinuities, treat a sharp re-entrant corner as singular and assess with a nominal/hot-spot stress or a modelled fillet with Kt): the beam-theory check and the converged buckling are right, and the author correctly flags sharp-corner mesh dependence. Departures: element-centroid averages on 2 and 4 elements across a bending section reported as 'peak stress'; the mesh-dependent rise attributed to the corner when most of it is sampling position; a pass declared on a mesh that misses half the bending stress; the 100 MPa working stress with no steel grade, yield or safety factor stated. A senior FE engineer would reject the stress columns as is and sign off only on the nominal-stress verdict.

verdict: Does not meet the bar. The arithmetic is honest and reproducible: run.py regenerates every number in results.txt; nominal stress, mass and deflection match my independent beam-theory and Castigliano checks; the forward buckling factor holds within 2% under refinement. The headline verdict (only the 1.5 mm design survives) is also right, because the nominal stress alone decides it. But the finite-element stress columns are centroid averages on 2 and 4 elements across a bending section, so they recover 50% and 75% of the outer-fibre stress. The README reads them as a sharp-corner effect, declares the 2.0 mm design a coarse-mesh pass and says the peaks overstate a filleted part, when they understate even the stress with no concentration. 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive the 3 tests, no outside prior work is cited, and the project is one more step in the simdesign cluster that PROGRAMMES.md names as fragmentation.
